units.title: Unit 63 — Cause, reason, purpose and result
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 132–133 (PDF pages 133–134).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Explain causes with accurate verb, noun and preposition patterns.
Distinguish expressions for the origin of an event, its motivation and its purpose.
Use formal written linkers to report results and consequences.
Select natural collocations and grammar patterns such as result in, reason for and with a view to.

items.example: The flight was delayed due to thick fog.
items.note: Introduces the cause; normally followed by a noun or noun phrase.

items.example: The sudden shutdown was caused by a power failure.
items.note: Passive pattern: something is caused by an event, action or condition.

items.example: The engineers are investigating the cause of the overheating.
items.note: Noun pattern: the cause of something. Distinguish cause (noun) from cause (verb).

items.example: A damaged cable caused the controller to restart.
items.note: Verb pattern: cause something; cause someone or something to do something.

items.example: Owing to a technical fault, the service was suspended.
items.note: A relatively formal alternative to because of; followed by a noun or noun phrase.

items.pt: devido ao fato de que; visto que
items.example: The test was postponed owing to the fact that the equipment was unavailable.
items.note: Use this longer form before a finite clause; do not place a bare clause directly after owing to.

items.example: The announcement sparked widespread protests.
items.note: Often used for a powerful or sudden reaction, including unrest, debate or conflict.

items.example: A controversial decision sparked off a public debate.
items.note: Phrasal-verb alternative to spark; often describes an intense reaction.

items.example: The new policy gave rise to several complaints.
items.note: Relatively formal; followed by a noun phrase, often criticism, concern or problems.

items.example: The minister’s remarks provoked a strong response.
items.note: Often collocates with criticism, opposition, anger or a reaction.

items.example: The report generated considerable interest among researchers.
items.note: Often used for effects such as interest, discussion, criticism or income.

items.example: The reforms brought about major changes in public transport.
items.note: Common with change, improvement or reform; often in political or social contexts.

items.example: Poor maintenance can lead to unexpected failures.
items.note: Follow with a noun or -ing form, not a bare infinitive: lead to failure / lead to failing.

items.example: Many of the delays stem from a shortage of skilled staff.
items.note: Highlights an underlying origin or source rather than just a visible consequence.

items.example: The dispute arose from a misunderstanding about the contract.
items.note: Used when a situation originates in an earlier event or circumstance; arise–arose–arisen.

items.example: Several legal questions arose out of the negotiations.
items.note: A more extended alternative to arise from; often used in formal writing.

items.example: Her reason for leaving was that she had accepted another position.
items.note: Use reason for + noun or -ing form: the reason for leaving.

items.pt: o motivo pelo qual; a razão pela qual
items.example: The reason why we cancelled the meeting was that the speaker was ill.
items.note: Common pattern: the reason (why) ... is/was that ...; do not use because after is.

items.example: The journalist questioned his motive for releasing the document.
items.note: A motive is an underlying reason or purpose for an action; often motive for + -ing.

items.example: The safety report prompted the team to revise its procedures.
items.note: Transitive pattern: something prompts someone to do something.

items.pt: com o objetivo de; visando a
items.example: We introduced the workshop with the aim of improving communication.
items.note: Formal purpose phrase; followed by a noun or -ing form, not a bare infinitive.

items.pt: com vistas a; com a intenção de
items.example: They met with a view to settling the disagreement.
items.note: Formal and rather indirect; to is a preposition and must be followed by a noun or -ing form.

items.pt: sob a justificativa de que; alegando que
items.example: The request was rejected on the grounds that the evidence was incomplete.
items.note: Formal reason or justification, especially in legal or institutional settings; followed by a clause.

items.pt: o objetivo de; a finalidade de
items.example: The purpose of the inspection is to identify hidden faults.
items.note: Pattern: the purpose of + noun or -ing form + is/was to + infinitive.

items.example: A supplier missed the deadline. As a result, production stopped.
items.note: Introduces a consequence of a previous event; usually set off by a comma at the start of a sentence.

items.example: The roads were flooded. As a consequence, schools remained closed.
items.note: More formal than as a result; usually refers back to the preceding event or situation.

items.example: The test data were incomplete. Consequently, the findings were inconclusive.
items.note: Formal written linker; it may begin a sentence followed by a comma.

items.example: The software fault resulted in several hours of downtime.
items.note: Verb + in + noun or -ing: result in delays / result in people waiting.

items.example: The outage was the result of an unexpected voltage drop.
items.note: Noun construction showing the effect of a previous cause.

items.example: A serious consequence of the decision was the loss of public confidence.
items.note: Often more formal than result; common pattern: a consequence of something.

items.example: The outcome of the negotiations surprised everyone.
items.note: Used for the final result of a process, meeting, discussion or sequence of events.

items.example: The upshot of the discussion was that we needed a new plan.
items.note: Less formal than outcome; especially common in the pattern the upshot was that ...

items.example: The announcement was made, and a heated argument ensued.
items.note: Very formal; means happen afterwards, often describing chaos, confusion or a dispute.

units.title: Unit 64 — Concession and contrast
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 134–135 (PDF pages 135–136).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Concede part of an argument using acknowledge, accept, admit and concede with appropriate register.
Distinguish conversational and formal ways of introducing contrasts and qualifications.
Use on the other hand for a different viewpoint and on the contrary to reject a claim.
Describe strong differences with established collocations such as poles apart and a yawning gap.

items.pt: concessão; reconhecimento de um ponto contrário
items.example: The introduction makes a concession before presenting a stronger argument.
items.note: Accepting one point while arguing that another point matters more.

items.example: Although the system is expensive, it is easy to maintain.
items.note: Conjunction introducing a concession; followed by a finite clause.

items.pt: mesmo assim; ainda assim; no entanto
items.example: The first trial failed. Nevertheless, the team continued testing.
items.note: Formal contrastive adverb, often separated by a comma.

items.example: The company acknowledged that customers had experienced delays.
items.note: Relatively formal; recognising a point does not necessarily mean accepting blame or liability.

items.example: I accept that you worked hard, but the report still needs revisions.
items.note: Less formal than acknowledge; can concede a point without agreeing with the conclusion.

items.example: I admit that I misunderstood the instructions.
items.note: Often acknowledges fault or an uncomfortable fact; admit (that) ... or admit doing something.

items.pt: reconhecer relutantemente; ceder em um argumento
items.example: She conceded that the proposal had some advantages.
items.note: Rather formal, common in debates when a speaker reluctantly yields one point.

items.pt: tudo muito bem, mas...; isso é ótimo, porém...
items.example: You've apologised, and that's all well and good, but the problem remains.
items.note: Informal; accepts a positive point before raising an objection or practical difficulty.

items.pt: tudo bem, mas...; isso é muito bom, porém...
items.example: You've prepared the slides, and that's all very well, but who will present them?
items.note: Informal phrase that acknowledges something but questions whether it is enough.

items.pt: é fácil dizer, mas...; tudo muito bem, mas...
items.example: It's all very well suggesting a new tool, but who will maintain it?
items.note: Often followed by an -ing form and a but-clause to criticise an impractical suggestion.

items.example: You shouldn't be surprised; after all, we warned you about the risks.
items.note: Introduces a reason the listener should already recognise; can soften an objection.

items.pt: apesar de tudo isso; mesmo assim
items.example: The candidate is inexperienced, but for all that, she has excellent ideas.
items.note: Concessive phrase: despite everything just mentioned; often follows but.

items.example: Admittedly, the upgrade was expensive, but it improved reliability.
items.note: More formal; signals that the speaker accepts a point before offering a qualification.

items.pt: o contrário é verdadeiro; ocorre o inverso
items.example: I expected sales to fall, but the reverse is true: they are rising.
items.note: Reverses a previously stated or expected situation; tense can change to was true.

items.example: We thought the task would be simple. In fact, it took three weeks.
items.note: Introduces the reality behind, or a correction to, an earlier statement or expectation.

items.example: The first design uses metal parts. In contrast, the second relies on plastic.
items.note: Marks a difference between two subjects or situations; commonly used in writing.

items.example: The flat is small. On the other hand, it is close to the station.
items.note: Adds another true consideration or viewpoint; it does not say the previous statement was false.

items.pt: muito pelo contrário; exatamente o oposto
items.example: I'm not disappointed; quite the opposite, I'm delighted with the result.
items.note: Strongly rejects an assumption by asserting the opposite is true.

items.example: The new version isn't less reliable. On the contrary, it's more stable than before.
items.note: Rejects or corrects the previous claim; unlike on the other hand, it says the earlier idea was untrue.

items.pt: quando se trata de; no que diz respeito a
items.example: When it comes to planning, the two managers have very different styles.
items.note: Introduces the topic about which people or things are being compared; to + noun or -ing form.

items.example: The two researchers are poles apart in their views on the proposal.
items.note: Describes extreme differences in views, values or approaches; often be poles apart.

items.pt: uma diferença enorme; uma diferença abismal
items.example: There is a world of difference between an estimate and a verified result.
items.note: A strong fixed expression; typically a world of difference between A and B.

items.pt: uma grande divisão; uma diferença profunda
items.example: There is a great divide between urban and rural voters on this issue.
items.note: Often refers to a serious social, political or ideological division.

items.example: A yawning gap remains between the highest and lowest wages.
items.note: Emphatic collocation for a very large disparity or separation, especially in wealth or opportunity.

items.pt: uma grande discrepância; uma diferença significativa
items.example: There is a huge discrepancy between the budget and the final cost.
items.note: A discrepancy is a mismatch between things expected to agree, such as figures or statements.

items.example: The supervisor agreed to take responsibility for the oversight.
items.note: Exercise 64.1 highlights conceding a point while assigning responsibility; take responsibility for + noun/-ing.

items.example: The supplier refused to accept liability for the damage.
items.note: Legal or corporate collocation; acknowledging a complaint is not the same as accepting liability.
